Asymptotic behavior of Eckhoff’s method for convergence acceleration of Dirac eigenfunction expansions

**Abstract**

The current paper considers the problem of recovering a vector-function on [-1,1] from a limited number of coefficients of its expansion into a series of eigenfunctions of a one- dimensional Dirac system. The Krylov-Lanczos-Eckhoff-Gottlieb acceleration method is examined in the situation when the boundary values it requires have to be computed from the generalized Fourier coefficients themselves. This leads to a \(2q\times 2q\) linear system whose matrix is a block Vandermonde matrix; its determinant and inverse are computed explicitly, and the asymptotic _L_<sub>2</sub>-error constant of the method is found, paralleling the classical trigonometric case.

## Introduction

Let \(\{\lambda_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\), \(\{v_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\) be the eigenvalues and _L_<sub>2</sub>-orthonormal eigenfunctions of a self-adjoint boundary value problem on a finite interval, and let _f_ be a square-integrable function on that interval. It is well known that the expansion

\(f(x)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty c_nv_n(x),c_n=\langle f,v_n\rangle,\)

converges to _f_ in _L_<sub>2</sub>. For practical purposes one approximates _f_ by the truncated series \(S_N(f)=\sum_{|n|\le N}c_nv_n\), and the involved error is strongly dependent on the smoothness of _f_. If _f_ belongs to the domain of the underlying differential operator, this approximation converges uniformly. If, however, _f_ or its derivatives do not satisfy the boundary conditions, the convergence becomes slow, its rate reflects only the smoothness of _f_, and the Gibbs phenomenon appears at the endpoints.

For the classical Fourier series \((v_n=e^{i\pi nx}/\sqrt{2}\) on [-1,1], the eigenfunctions of _id/dx_ with periodic boundary conditions), increasing the convergence rate by subtracting a polynomial that carries the discontinuities of the function and of its first few derivatives was suggested by A. Krylov as early as 1906 [13] and later, in 1964, by C. Lanczos [14, 15]. More detailed investigation of this approach, together with practical algorithms for computing the "jumps" of _f_ and its derivatives from the Fourier coefficients alone, was performed by K. S. Eckhoff and D. Gottlieb [6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]. The method is now usually called the Krylov-Lanczos- Eckhoff-Gottlieb, or simply Eckhoff, method. Its asymptotic _L_<sub>2</sub> error constants were computed by A. Barkhudaryan, R. Barkhudaryan and A. Poghosyan in [1]. An alternative acceleration technique for nonperiodic functions, based on quasi-periodic approximations and interpolations, was developed in [22, 23, 21].

For more general self-adjoint boundary value problems, in particular for Sturm-Liouville and Dirac systems, the analogue of Krylov’s correction polynomial is no longer a Bernoulli polynomial but a combination of derivatives of the Green’s function of the underlying operator. The basic algebraic identity behind the method, an integration-by-parts decomposition of _c<sub>n</sub>_ into a boundary part _P<sub>n</sub>_ and a smoother interior part _F<sub>n</sub>_, was extended by J. Shaw, L. Johnson and R. Riess \[24\] and, in the form most relevant here, by A. Nersessian and A. Poghosyan \[18, 20, 19\]. The Gibbs phenomenon in eigenfunction expansions of the one-dimensional Dirac system was studied in \[4\]. For the same system, by R. Barkhudaryan obtained in \[2, 3\] a generalization of the Eckhoff method under the assumption that the boundary values of _f_ and of its successive Dirac iterates are known _exactly_, and computed the asymptotic _L_<sub>2</sub> constant of the resulting approximation.

In the current paper we consider the case when these boundary values are not known in advance and have to be _computed_ from the Fourier coefficients \(\{c_n\}_{|n|\le N}\) themselves, exactly as Eckhoff proposed in the trigonometric case. The boundary conditions on the eigenfunctions reduce the 4_q_ scalar boundary values of _f_ to 2_q reduced boundary values_ \(g_k^\pm\), and Eckhoff’s recipe, applied at 2_q_ selected indices _n<sub>s</sub>_, leads to a linear system for their approximations \(\widetilde{g}_k^\pm\) -- the KEG-D system -- whose coefficient matrix is a \(2q\times 2q\) _block Vandermonde matrix_, the natural generalization of the \(q\times q\) Vandermonde matrix of the original Eckhoff method. Accordingly, in Section 1 we recall the Dirac boundary value problem and the exact-jumps form of the convergence acceleration of \[2\]; in Section 2 we prove a closed-form expression for the determinant of the block Vandermonde matrix and describe its inverse; in Section 3 we set up the KEG-D system and estimate the errors \(\widetilde{g}_k^\pm-g_k^\pm\), showing in particular that strict parity balance is necessary and sufficient for the leading-order coefficient matrix to be nonsingular; and in Section 4 we prove the main result of the paper (Theorem 4.1), an explicit formula for the limit of \(N^{2q+1}\|\widetilde{R}_{q,N}(f)\|^2\) in terms of the Dirac jump constants.

## 1 The Dirac system and exact-jumps method

We work with the canonical Dirac system on \[-1,1\]<tbc>

\(\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
0 & 1 \\
-1 & 0
\end{array}\right)\frac{dy}{dx}-\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
p(x) & 0 \\
0 & r(x)
\end{array}\right)y=\lambda y,\) (1)

<tbc>with separated self-adjoint boundary conditions

\(y_2(-1)cos\alpha+y_1(-1)sin\alpha=0,y_2(1)cos\beta+y_1(1)sin\beta=0,\) (2)

where \(p,r\in C^1[-1,1]\) are real-valued and \(\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi]\). We assume that \(\lambda=0\) is not an eigenvalue. This entails no loss of generality, since the spectrum is discrete and a constant spectral shift may always be made so that zero does not belong to the spectrum.

Let \(\{\lambda_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\) be the eigenvalues, indexed in increasing order, with the origin of the indexing chosen consistently with the asymptotic formula below, so that \(\lambda_n\rightarrow\pm\infty\) as \(n\rightarrow\pm\infty\). Let {_v<sub>n</sub>_} be the corresponding real orthonormal eigenfunctions in _L_<sub>2</sub>(\[-1,1\];R<sup>2</sup>). The asymptotic results of Levitan-Sargsyan \[16\] give

\(v_{n,1}(x)=K_0cos(\xi_n(x)-\alpha)+O(1/n),v_{n,2}(x)=K_0sin(\xi_n(x)-\alpha)+O(1/n),\) (3)

as \(n\rightarrow\pm\infty\), uniformly for \(x\in[-1,1]\), where

\(\xi_n(x):=\lambda_n(x+1)+\frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^x\left(p(\tau)+r(\tau)\right)d\tau.\) (4)

Choosing the sign of each eigenfunction so that the leading coefficient is positive, the _L_2- normalization determines \(K_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\) since (3) yields \(\|v_n\|_{L_2}^2=\int_{-1}^1\left(v_{n,1}^2(x)+v_{n,2}^2(x)\right)dx=2K_0^2+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)=1.\) Moreover, the eigenvalues satisfy \[16\] \(\lambda_n=\frac{\pi n}{2}-\frac{\widetilde{\theta}}{2}+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),n\rightarrow\pm\infty,\) (5) where \(\widetilde{\theta}:=\beta-\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^1(p(\tau)+r(\tau))d\tau.\) ## 1.1 Reduced boundary values The eigenfunctions satisfy the boundary conditions (2) exactly. Hence, their endpoint values belong to the corresponding one-dimensional boundary subspaces: \(v_n(1)=\kappa_n^{(+)}\left(\begin{array}{ c } cos\beta \\ -sin\beta \end{array}\right),v_n(-1)=\kappa_n^{(-)}\left(\begin{array}{ c } cos\alpha \\ -sin\alpha \end{array}\right),\) (6) for some real scalars \(\kappa_n^{(\pm)}\). We set \(\mathcal{A}f:=Jf'-Qf,J=\left(\begin{array}{ c c } 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{array}\right),Q(x)=\text{diag}(p(x),r(x)),\) and define \(\mathcal{B}f:=-Jf=\left(\begin{array}{ c } -f_2 \\ f_1 \end{array}\right),f_k:=\mathcal{B}\mathcal{A}^kf=-J\mathcal{A}^kf,k\ge 0.\) (7) Thus, \(\mathcal{A}^kf=\left(\begin{array}{ c c } (\mathcal{A}^kf)_1 & \\ (\mathcal{A}^kf)_2 \end{array}\right),f_k=\left(\begin{array}{ c } -(\mathcal{A}^kf)_2 \\ (\mathcal{A}^kf)_1 \end{array}\right).\) For the remainder of this subsection, let \(q\ge 1\) and assume in addition that \(f\in C^q([-1,1];\mathbb{R}^2),p,r\in C^q[-1,1],\) so that A_kf_ is continuous for _k_=0_,...,q_. For _k_=0_,...,q_, we define the _reduced boundary values_ \(g_k^\pm:=f_{k,1}(\pm 1)cos\gamma_\pm-f_{k,2}(\pm 1)sin\gamma_\pm,\gamma_+=\beta,\gamma_-=\alpha.\) (8) Equivalently, \(g_k^\pm=-(\mathcal{A}^kf)_2(\pm 1)cos\gamma_\pm-(\mathcal{A}^kf)_1(\pm 1)sin\gamma_\pm.\) By (6), the boundary terms involving the eigenfunctions reduce to \(v_n^T(\pm 1)f_k(\pm 1)=\kappa_n^{(\pm)}\left(cos\gamma_\pm-sin\gamma_\pm\right)\left(\begin{array}{ c } f_{k,1}(\pm 1) \\ f_{k,2}(\pm 1) \end{array}\right)\)
\(=\kappa_n^{(\pm)}g_k^\pm.\)

It remains to determine the asymptotic behavior of \(\kappa_n^{(\pm)}\). By (4) and (5), \(\xi_n(1)-\alpha=n\pi-\beta+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),\xi_n(-1)-\alpha=-\alpha.\) Substituting these relations into (3) gives \(v_n(1)=K_0(-1)^n\genfrac(){pt}{2}{cos\beta}{-sin\beta}+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),\) and \(v_n(-1)=K_0\genfrac(){pt}{2}{cos\alpha}{-sin\alpha}+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right).\) Since the boundary-direction vectors in (6) have unit norm, taking the scalar product with the corresponding direction in the above asymptotic formulas and using (6) yields \(\kappa_n^{(+)}=K_0(-1)^n+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),\kappa_n^{(-)}=K_0+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right).\) (9) ## 1.2 Approximation with exact boundary corrections For \(q\ge 1\), let \(f\in C^q([-1,1];\mathbb{R}^2),p,r\in C^q[-1,1].\) Define the generalized Fourier coefficients of _f_ with respect to the orthonormal Dirac eigenfunctions \(\{v_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\) by \(c_n:=\langle f,v_n\rangle_{L_2}=\int_{-1}^1v_n^T(x)f(x)dx.\) We first derive a one-step integration-by-parts identity. Since \(\mathcal{A}v_n=\lambda_nv_n\), for any sufficiently regular vector-valued function _h_, \(\lambda_n\int_{-1}^1v_n^Thdx=\int_{-1}^1(\mathcal{A}v_n)^Thdx.\) Using \(\mathcal{A}v_n=Jv'_n-Qv_n\), _JT_=-_J_, _QT=Q_, we obtain \(\int_{-1}^1(\mathcal{A}v_n)^Thdx=\int_{-1}^1\left(-v'_n^TJh-v_n^TQh\right)dx\)
\(=-\left[v_n^TJh\right]_{-1}^1+\int_{-1}^1v_n^T(Jh'-Qh)dx\)
\(=v_n^T(-1)Jh(-1)-v_n^T(1)Jh(1)+\int_{-1}^1v_n^T\mathcal{A}hdx.\) Therefore, \(\int_{-1}^1v_n^Thdx=\lambda_n^{-1}\left[v_n^T(-1)Jh(-1)-v_n^T(1)Jh(1)\right]+\lambda_n^{-1}\int_{-1}^1v_n^T\mathcal{A}hdx.\) (10) We now apply (10) with _h_=A_kf_. Using (7), (6) and the definition (8), \(v_n^T(-1)J\mathcal{A}^kf(-1)-v_n^T(1)J\mathcal{A}^kf(1)\)
\(=-v_n^T(-1)f_k(-1)+v_n^T(1)f_k(1)\)
\(=-\kappa_n^{(-)}g_k^-+\kappa_n^{(+)}g_k^+.\)

Define<tbc>

\(x_n:=\frac{1}{\lambda_n}.\)

<tbc>Then<tbc>

\(\int_{-1}^1v_n^T\mathcal{A}^kfdx=x_n(\kappa_n^{(+)}g_k^+-\kappa_n^{(-)}g_k^-)+x_n\int_{-1}^1v_n^T\mathcal{A}^{k+1}fdx.\) (11)

<tbc>Starting with _k_=0 and iterating (11) _q_ times yields<tbc>

\(c_n=P_n+F_n,\) (12)

<tbc>where<tbc>

\(P_n=x_n\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}x_n^k(\kappa_n^{(+)}g_k^+-\kappa_n^{(-)}g_k^-),F_n=\lambda_n^{-q}\int_{-1}^1v_n^T(x)\mathcal{A}^qf(x)dx.\) (13)

<tbc>If, in addition, _f_<sup>(_q_)</sup> is absolutely continuous, one more integration by parts, combined with the asymptotics (3) and the Riemann-Lebesgue theorem (cf. \[2\]), gives the sharper expansion<tbc>

\(F_n=x_n^{q+1}\left[\kappa_n^{(+)}g_q^+-\kappa_n^{(-)}g_q^-\right]+o(|n|^{-q-1}),|n|\rightarrow\infty.\) (14)

<tbc>Following \[2\] we define the exact-jumps approximation<tbc>

\(S_{q,N}(f):=P(x)+\sum_{|n|\le N}F_nv_n(x),\) (15)

\(P(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}\big[G_k(x,1,0)f_k(1)-G_k(x,-1,0)f_k(-1)\big],\)

<tbc>where<tbc>

\(G_k(x,\xi,0)=\frac{1}{k!}\partial_\lambda^kG(x,\xi,\lambda)\big|_{\lambda=0},\)

<tbc>with _G_ denoting the Green’s matrix of (1)-(2). By the spectral representation of the Green’s matrix and its derivatives, the generalized Fourier coefficient of _P_ corresponding to _v<sub>n</sub>_ is precisely _P<sub>n</sub>_, that is,<tbc>

\(\int_{-1}^1v_n^T(x)P(x)dx=P_n.\)

<tbc>Substituting (9) into (14) and using the reduced boundary values \(g_q^\pm\) defined in (8),<tbc>

\(F_n=K_0x_n^{q+1}\big[(-1)^nA+B\big]+o(|n|^{-q-1}),\) (16)

<tbc>with the _Dirac jump constants_

\(A:=g_q^+=f_{q,1}(1)\mathrm{cos}\beta-f_{q,2}(1)\mathrm{sin}\beta,B:=-g_q^-=f_{q,2}(-1)\mathrm{sin}\alpha-f_{q,1}(-1)\mathrm{cos}\alpha.\) (17)

<tbc>Hence, by (12), the generalized Fourier coefficients of _f-P_ are precisely _F<sub>n</sub>_. Consequently,<tbc>

\(R_{q,N}(f)=f-S_{q,N}(f)=\sum_{|n|>N}F_nv_n.\)

<tbc>By Parseval and (16),

\(\mathrm{lim}_{N\rightarrow\infty} N^{2q+1}\|R_{q,N}(f)\|^2=\frac{2^{2q+2}}{\pi^{2q+2}(2q+1)}(A^2+B^2),\) (18)

where the constant is obtained by a Riemann-sum argument applied to

\(\sum_{|n|>N}K_0^2x_n^{2q+2}[(-1)^nA+B]^2,\)

split by parity (see the proof of Theorem 4.1), using \(K_0^2=1/2\). The formula (18) replaces Theorem 2 of \[2\]: the constant \(2^{2q+3}/\pi^{2q+3}\) stated there must be replaced by \(2^{2q+2}/\pi^{2q+2}\), in accordance with \(K_0^2=1/2\) rather than \(1/\pi\), and the boundary directions entering the constant _A_ there involve an extraneous angle \(2\theta-\beta\); the corrected constants are (17).

The approximation (15) has a serious drawback: it assumes the boundary values \(f_k(\pm 1)\) to be known in advance, while in many applications they are not. In the next two sections we develop the tools needed to compute them from the generalized Fourier coefficients themselves.

## 2 Block Vandermonde matrices

In this section, we study the algebraic structure of the coefficient matrix arising in the linear system used to approximate the reduced boundary values.

**Definition 2.1.** Let \(q\in\mathbb{N}\), and let \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{2q}\), \(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_{2q}\), and _x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x_<sub>2_q_</sub> be complex numbers. We define the _block Vandermonde matrix of order_ 2_q_ to be the following \(2q\times 2q\) matrix:

\(\Lambda=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c c c c }
\alpha_1 & \alpha_1x_1 & \cdots & \alpha_1x_1^{q-1} & \beta_1 & \beta_1x_1 & \cdots & \beta_1x_1^{q-1} \\
\alpha_2 & \alpha_2x_2 & \cdots & \alpha_2x_2^{q-1} & \beta_2 & \beta_2x_2 & \cdots & \beta_2x_2^{q-1} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
\alpha_{2q} & \alpha_{2q}x_{2q} & \cdots & \alpha_{2q}x_{2q}^{q-1} & \beta_{2q} & \beta_{2q}x_{2q} & \cdots & \beta_{2q}x_{2q}^{q-1}
\end{array}\right).\) (19)

Let<tbc>

\(V_q=\left(x_i^{j-1}\right)_{1\le i\le 2q,1\le j\le q}\)

<tbc>denote the rectangular \(2q\times q\) Vandermonde matrix, and let<tbc>

\(D_\alpha=\text{diag}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{2q}),D_\beta=\text{diag}(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_{2q}).\)

<tbc>Then<tbc>

\(\Lambda=\left(D_\alpha V_q|D_\beta V_q\right)=BC,B=\left(D_\alpha|D_\beta\right),C=\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
V_q & 0 \\
0 & V_q
\end{array}\right).\) (20)

<tbc>Here,<tbc>

\(B\in\mathbb{C}^{2q\times 4q},C\in\mathbb{C}^{4q\times 2q}.\)

<tbc>For a subset \(T\subseteq[2q]:=\{1,\dots,2q\}\), write<tbc>

\(T=\{t_1<\cdots<t_m\},m=|T|,\)

<tbc>and define the square Vandermonde matrix associated with _T_ by<tbc>

\(V_T=\left(x_{t_i}^{j-1}\right)_{1\le i,j\le m}.\)

<tbc>Its determinant is

\(\text{det}(V_T)=\prod_{1\le i<j\le m}\left(x_{t_j}-x_{t_i}\right).\)

The factorization (20) allows us to compute the determinant of \(\Lambda\) systematically by means of the Cauchy-Binet formula.

## 2.1 Determinant

**Theorem 2.2.** _The determinant of the block Vandermonde matrix_ (19) _is_<tbc>

\(det\Lambda=\sum_{T\subseteq[2q]|T|=q}\varepsilon(T)\left(\prod_{i\in T}\alpha_i\right)\left(\prod_{j\in T^c}\beta_j\right)det(V_T)det(V_{T^c}),\) (21)

<tbc>_where, for each_<tbc>

\(T=\{t_1<\cdots<t_q\},T^c=[2q]\backslash T=\{u_1<\cdots<u_q\},\)

<tbc>_we set_<tbc>

\(\varepsilon(T):=(-1)\sum_{k=1}^q(t_k-k).\)

<tbc>_Equivalently,_<tbc>

\(det\Lambda=\sum_{T\subseteq[2q]|T|=q}\varepsilon(T)\left(\prod_{i\in T}\alpha_i\right)\left(\prod_{j\in T^c}\beta_j\right)\prod_{1\le i<j\le q}(x_{t_j}-x_{t_i})\prod_{1\le i<j\le q}(x_{u_j}-x_{u_i}).\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Applying the Cauchy-Binet formula (see, for example, \[10\]) to the factorization \(\Lambda=BC\) in (20), we have

\(det\Lambda=\sum_{S\subseteq[4q]|S|=2q}det(B_{[:,S]})det(C_{[S,:]}),\)

where _B_<sub>\[:,_S_\]</sub> denotes the submatrix of _B_ formed by all rows and the columns indexed by _S_, while _C_<sub>\[_S,_:\]</sub> denotes the submatrix of _C_ formed by the rows indexed by _S_ and all columns.

A subset \(S\subseteq[4q]\) with |_S_|=2_q_ can contribute only if _B_<sub>\[:,_S_\]</sub> is nonsingular. Each column of _B_ is a scalar multiple of a standard basis vector **e**_<sub>i</sub>_: column _i_ is \(\alpha_i\mathbf{e}_i\), while column 2_q+i_ is \(\beta_i\mathbf{e}_i\). Hence _B_<sub>\[:,_S_\]</sub> is nonsingular only if exactly one column is selected from each pair {_i,_2_q+i_}, _i_=1_,...,_2_q_.

Define<tbc>

\(T:=S\cap[2q].\)

<tbc>Since exactly one element is selected from each pair {_i,_2_q+i_}, \(i\in[2q]\), we have<tbc>

\(T^c:=[2q]\backslash T=\{i\in[2q]:2q+i\in S\}.\)

<tbc>Since the indices in the first block of _C_ precede those in the second block, the submatrix _C_<sub>\[_S,_:\]</sub> has the block-diagonal form<tbc>

\(C_{[S,:]}=\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
\left(x_i^{j-1}\right)_{1\le j\le q} & 0 \\
0 & \left(x_i^{j-1}\right)_{1\le j\le q}
\end{array}\right).\)

<tbc>If _C_<sub>\[_S,_:\]</sub> is nonsingular, then its first _q_ columns must be linearly independent. Since these columns are supported only in the first |_T_| rows, this requires \(|T|\ge q\). Likewise, the last _q_ columns are supported only in the remaining 2_q_-|_T_| rows, so their linear independence requires

\(2q-|T|\ge q.\)

Hence \(|T|\le q\), and therefore |_T_|=_q_. Thus both diagonal blocks are the square Vandermonde matrices _V<sub>T</sub>_ and _V<sub>T<sup>c</sup></sub>_.

For each _q_-element subset \(T\subseteq[2q]\), the corresponding set _S_ is uniquely determined. If<tbc>

\(T=\{t_1<\cdots<t_q\},T^c=\{u_1<\cdots<u_q\},\)

then the selected columns of _B_ occur in the order<tbc>

\(\alpha_{t_1}\mathbf{e}_{t_1},\dots,\alpha_{t_q}\mathbf{e}_{t_q},\beta_{u_1}\mathbf{e}_{u_1},\dots,\beta_{u_q}\mathbf{e}_{u_q}.\)

<tbc>The sign of the corresponding permutation is<tbc>

\(\varepsilon(T)=(-1)\sum_{k=1}^q(t_k-k).\)

<tbc>Hence<tbc>

\(det(B_{[:,S]})=\varepsilon(T)\left(\prod_{i\in T}\alpha_i\right)\left(\prod_{j\in T^c}\beta_j\right),\)

<tbc>while

\(det(C_{[S,:]})=det(V_T)det(V_{T^c}).\)

Summing over all subsets \(T\subseteq[2q]\) with |_T_|=_q_ gives (21).

**Corollary 2.3.** _The matrix_ \(\Lambda\) _is invertible if and only if the right-hand side of_ (21) _is non-zero. In particular,_ \(\Lambda\) _is singular whenever_ \(\alpha_i=\beta_i\) _for all i._

_Proof._ The invertibility criterion follows immediately from Theorem 2.2. If \(\alpha_i=\beta_i\) for all _i_, then the _j_-th columns of the two blocks in (19) coincide, so \(\Lambda\) is singular. (Note that this is not visible term by term in (21): the terms of _T_ and _T<sup>c</sup>_ cancel in pairs only for odd _q_, since \(\varepsilon(T^c)=(-1)^q\varepsilon(T).\))

## 2.2 Inverse via polynomial interpolation

**Theorem 2.4.** _Suppose that_ \(det(\Lambda)\neq 0\)_, and write_<tbc>

\(\Lambda^{-1}=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{Y}{Z},Y,Z\in\mathbb{C}^{q\times 2q}.\)

<tbc>_For each j_=1_,...,_2_q, define the polynomials_<tbc>

\(Y_j(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}Y_{k+1,j}x^k,Z_j(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}Z_{k+1,j}x^k.\)

<tbc>_Then_ (_Y<sub>j</sub>,Z<sub>j</sub>_) _is the unique pair of polynomials of degree at most q_-1 _satisfying_

\(\alpha_iY_j(x_i)+\beta_iZ_j(x_i)=\delta_{ij},i=1,\dots,2q.\) (22)

_Proof._ Let **y**_<sub>j</sub>_ and **z**_<sub>j</sub>_ denote the _j_-th columns of _Y_ and _Z_, respectively. The _j_-th column of the identity \(\Lambda\Lambda^{-1}=I_{2q}\) gives<tbc>

\(D_\alpha V_q\mathbf{y}_j+D_\beta V_q\mathbf{z}_j=\mathbf{e}_j.\)

<tbc>By the definitions of _Y<sub>j</sub>_ and _Z<sub>j</sub>_, the _i_-th component of this identity is

\(\alpha_iY_j(x_i)+\beta_iZ_j(x_i)=\delta_{ij},\)

which proves (22).

Conversely, any pair of polynomials of degree at most _q_-1 satisfying (22) determines coefficient vectors \(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{C}^q\) satisfying

\(\Lambda\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\mathbf{y}}{\mathbf{z}}=\mathbf{e}_j.\)

Since \(\Lambda\) is invertible, this system has a unique solution. Hence the pair (_Y<sub>j</sub>,Z<sub>j</sub>_) is unique.

## 2.3 An explicit cofactor formula

For \(j\in[2q]\), let<tbc>

\(R_j:=[2q]\backslash\{j\},\)

<tbc>equipped with the natural order inherited from \[2_q_\]. Define the order isomorphism<tbc>

\(\rho_j:R_j\rightarrow[2q-1]\)

<tbc>by<tbc>

\(\rho_j(i):=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
i, & i<j, \\
i-1, & i>j.
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>For a subset<tbc>

\(T=\{t_1<\cdots<t_s\}\subseteq R_j,s=|T|,\)

<tbc>let<tbc>

\(T':=R_j\backslash T.\)

<tbc>We define the shuffle sign \(\varepsilon_j(T)\) by

\(\varepsilon_j(T):=(-1)\sum_{k=1}^s(\rho_j(t_k)-k)=(-1)^{\#\{(u,t)\in T^\prime\times T:u<t\}}.\)

Equivalently, \(\varepsilon_j(T)\) is the sign of the shuffle permutation of the ordered set _R<sub>j</sub>_ that places the elements of _T_ before the elements of \(T'\), while preserving the natural order within each set.

For any index set<tbc>

\(S=\{s_1<\cdots<s_d\}\subseteq[2q]\)

<tbc>and exponent set<tbc>

\(E=\{e_1<\cdots<e_d\}\subset\mathbb{N}_0,\)

<tbc>we denote the generalized Vandermonde matrix by<tbc>

\(V_S^E:=\left(x_{s_i}^{e_k}\right)_{1\le i,k\le d}.\)

<tbc>For variables _y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,y<sub>d</sub>_, let<tbc>

\(e_r(y_1,\dots,y_d)=\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_r\le d}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_r}\)

<tbc>denote the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree _r_, with the conventions

\(e_0=1,e_r=0\text{for}r<0\text{or}r>d.\)

For \(T\subseteq[2q]\), we write

\(e_r((x_t)_{t\in T})\)

for the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree _r_ in the variables _x<sub>t</sub>_, \(t\in T\).

We also adopt the standard convention that empty products and determinants of \(0\times 0\) matrices equal 1.

For _r_=1_,...,q_, set<tbc>

\(E_r:=\{0,1,\dots,q-1\}\backslash\{r-1\}.\)

<tbc>For \(1\le j,m\le 2q\), let _M<sub>j,m</sub>_ denote the minor obtained from \(\Lambda\) by deleting row _j_ and column _m_. If \(det(\Lambda)\neq 0\), then the standard cofactor formula gives<tbc>

\((\Lambda^{-1})_{m,j}=\frac{(-1)^{j+m}}{det(\Lambda)}M_{j,m}.\)

**Theorem 2.5.** _Fix_ \(j\in[2q]\).

_If_ \(1\le m\le q\)_, then_

\(M_{j,m}=\sum_{T\subseteq R_j|T|=q-1}\varepsilon_j(T)\left(\prod_{i\in T}\alpha_i\right)\left(\prod_{i\in T^\prime}\beta_i\right)\mathrm{det}\left(V_T^{E_m}\right)\mathrm{det}(V_{T^\prime}),\) (23)

_where_

\(\mathrm{det}\left(V_T^{E_m}\right)=\prod_{r<sr,s\in T}(x_s-x_r)e_{q-m}((x_t)_{t\in T}).\) (24)

_If_ \(m=q+\ell\), \(1\le\ell\le q\)_, then_

\(M_{j,q+\ell}=\sum_{T\subseteq R_j|T|=q}\varepsilon_j(T)\left(\prod_{i\in T}\alpha_i\right)\left(\prod_{i\in T^\prime}\beta_i\right)\mathrm{det}(V_T)\mathrm{det}\left(V_{T^\prime}^{E_\ell}\right),\) (25)

_where_

\(\mathrm{det}\left(V_{T^\prime}^{E_\ell}\right)=\prod_{r<sr,s\in T^\prime}(x_s-x_r)e_{q-\ell}((x_t)_{t\in T^\prime}).\) (26)

_Proof._ We compute the minors _M<sub>j,m</sub>_. First suppose that \(1\le m\le q\), so that the deleted column belongs to the \(\alpha\)-block. After deleting row _j_ and column _m_, the remaining rows are indexed by _R<sub>j</sub>_. The remaining \(\alpha\)-block has exponent set _E<sub>m</sub>_, while the \(\beta\)-block still has exponent set

\(\{0,1,\dots,q-1\}.\)

Applying the same Cauchy-Binet argument as in the proof of Theorem 2.2 to the matrix obtained after deleting row _j_ and column _m_, a nonzero term is obtained by assigning _q_-1 indices to the \(\alpha\)-block and _q_ indices to the \(\beta\)-block. Hence the contributing subsets are precisely

\(T\subseteq R_j,|T|=q-1.\)

Then \(|T'|=q\). The indices in _T_ contribute to the \(\alpha\)-block, while the indices in \(T'\) contribute to the \(\beta\)-block.

For a fixed _T_, the diagonal weights contribute

\(\left(\prod_{i\in T}\alpha_i\right)\left(\prod_{i\in T^\prime}\beta_i\right).\)

The associated shuffle places the elements of _T_ before the elements of \(T'\), while preserving the natural order within each set. By definition, the sign of this shuffle is

\(\varepsilon_j(T)=(-1)\sum_{k=1}^{q-1}(\rho_j(t_k)-k),T=\{t_1<\cdots<t_{q-1}\}.\)

The polynomial part contributes

\(\mathrm{det}\left(V_T^{E_m}\right)\text{and}\mathrm{det}(V_{T^\prime}).\)

Therefore

\(M_{j,m}=\sum_{T\subseteq R_j|T|=q-1}\varepsilon_j(T)\left(\prod_{i\in T}\alpha_i\right)\left(\prod_{i\in T^\prime}\beta_i\right)\mathrm{det}\left(V_T^{E_m}\right)\mathrm{det}(V_{T^\prime}).\)

This proves (23).

It remains to evaluate \(\mathrm{det}(V_T^{E_m})\). By the classical alternant formula for Schur polynomials (see, for example, \[17\]), the generalized Vandermonde determinant factors as the ordinary Vandermonde determinant times the Schur polynomial associated with the exponent set. For _E<sub>m</sub>_, this Schur polynomial is the elementary symmetric polynomial _e_<sub>_q-m_</sub>. Hence

\(\mathrm{det}\big(V_T^{E_m}\big)=\prod_{r<sr,s\in T}(x_s-x_r)e_{q-m}((x_t)_{t\in T}).\)

This proves (24).

Now suppose that<tbc>

\(m=q+\ell,1\le\ell\le q.\)

<tbc>Then the deleted column belongs to the \(\beta\)-block. The \(\alpha\)-block keeps the full exponent set<tbc>

\(\{0,1,\dots,q-1\},\)

<tbc>whereas the \(\beta\)-block has exponent set \(E_\ell\). Thus a nonzero Cauchy–Binet term must assign _q_ indices to the \(\alpha\)-block and _q_-1 indices to the \(\beta\)-block. Hence the contributing subsets satisfy<tbc>

\(T\subseteq R_j,|T|=q.\)

<tbc>Then \(|T'|=q-1\). The same shuffle-sign argument gives

\(M_{j,q+\ell}=\sum_{T\subseteq R_j|T|=q}\varepsilon_j(T)\left(\prod_{i\in T}\alpha_i\right)\left(\prod_{i\in T^\prime}\beta_i\right)\mathrm{det}(V_T)\mathrm{det}\big(V_{T^\prime}^{E_\ell}\big).\)

This proves (25).

Similarly, the same alternant formula gives

\(\mathrm{det}\big(V_{T^\prime}^{E_\ell}\big)=\prod_{r<sr,s\in T^\prime}(x_s-x_r)e_{q-\ell}((x_t)_{t\in T^\prime}).\)

This proves (26) and completes the proof.

**Remark 2.6.** For large _q_ the \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{2q}{q}\) terms in (21) are too numerous for the determinant formula to be useful for numerical computation. In practice, one may solve the system

\(\Lambda\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{e}_j\)

by Gaussian elimination, which requires _O(q_<sup>3</sup>) operations. For ordinary Vandermonde systems, specialized algorithms such as the Björck–Pereyra algorithm reduce the computational complexity; see, for example, \[5\]. Whether the particular block Vandermonde structure of (19) can be exploited to obtain a comparable fast algorithm is an interesting numerical question, which we do not pursue here.

## 3 The KEG-D system with approximate boundary values

### 3.1 Setting up the system

Let \(q\ge 1\), let<tbc>

\(f\in C^q([-1,1];\mathbb{R}^2),p,r\in C^q[-1,1],\)

<tbc>and assume that _f_<sup>(_q_)</sup> is absolutely continuous. For sufficiently large _N_, choose 2_q_ distinct indices \(n_1,\dots,n_{2q}\in\mathbb{Z}\backslash\{0\}\) satisfying

\(\alpha_0N\le|n_s|\le N,s=1,\dots,2q,\) (27)

for some fixed constant \(0<\alpha_0<1\), and form the following linear system, obtained by discarding the remainder term _F<sub>n<sub>s</sub></sub>_ in (12)-(13):<tbc>

\(c_{n_s}=x_{n_s}\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}x_{n_s}^k[\kappa_{n_s}^{(+)}\widetilde{g}_k^+-\kappa_{n_s}^{(-)}\widetilde{g}_k^-],s=1,\dots,2q.\) (28)

<tbc>Introducing the polynomial pair<tbc>

\(\widetilde{G}^+(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}\widetilde{g}_k^+x^k,\widetilde{G}^-(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}\widetilde{g}_k^-x^k,\mathrm{deg}\widetilde{G}^\pm\le q-1,\)

<tbc>we can rewrite the system (28) as the interpolation problem<tbc>

\(\kappa_{n_s}^{(+)}\widetilde{G}^+(x_{n_s})-\kappa_{n_s}^{(-)}\widetilde{G}^-(x_{n_s})=\lambda_{n_s}c_{n_s},s=1,\dots,2q.\) (29)

<tbc>The coefficient matrix of (29) is<tbc>

\(\Lambda_N:=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c c c c }
\kappa_{n_1}^{(+)} & \kappa_{n_1}^{(+)}x_{n_1} & \cdots & \kappa_{n_1}^{(+)}x_{n_1}^{q-1} & -\kappa_{n_1}^{(-)} & -\kappa_{n_1}^{(-)}x_{n_1} & \cdots & -\kappa_{n_1}^{(-)}x_{n_1}^{q-1} \\
\vdots & \vdots &  & \vdots &  & \vdots &  & \vdots &  & \vdots \\
\kappa_{n_2q}^{(+)} & \kappa_{n_2q}^{(+)}x_{n_2q} & \cdots & \kappa_{n_2q}^{(+)}x_{n_2q}^{q-1} & -\kappa_{n_2q}^{(-)} & -\kappa_{n_2q}^{(-)}x_{n_2q} & \cdots & -\kappa_{n_2q}^{(-)}x_{n_2q}^{q-1}
\end{array}\right).\)

<tbc>Thus, \(\Lambda_N\) is the block Vandermonde matrix (19) with the identification

\(\alpha_s:=\kappa_{n_s}^{(+)},\beta_s:=-\kappa_{n_s}^{(-)},x_s:=x_{n_s}.\)

Since \(\lambda_{n_s}\neq 0\), multiplying the _s_-th equation of (28) by \(\lambda_{n_s}\) does not change its solvability. Thus (28) and (29) are equivalent linear systems, and \(\Lambda_N\) is the coefficient matrix of the latter. Theorem 2.2 therefore gives an explicit criterion for the unique solvability of (28). By Theorem 2.4, when \(\Lambda_N\) is invertible, the solution is the unique pair of polynomials \(\widetilde{G}^\pm\) of degree at most _q_-1 satisfying (29).

## 3.2 Error polynomials

Comparing (28) with (12)-(13), we see that the error polynomials<tbc>

\(\Delta^\pm(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}(\widetilde{g}_k^\pm-g_k^\pm)x^k(\mathrm{deg}\le q-1)\)

<tbc>satisfy

\(\kappa_{n_s}^{(+)}\Delta^+(x_{n_s})-\kappa_{n_s}^{(-)}\Delta^-(x_{n_s})=\lambda_{n_s}F_{n_s},s=1,\dots,2q.\) (30)

From (30) and (14), setting

\(\Phi^\pm(x):=\Delta^\pm(x)-g_q^\pm x^q(\mathrm{deg}\le q),\) (31)

the system becomes the almost homogeneous system

\(\kappa_{n_s}^{(+)}\Phi^+(x_{n_s})-\kappa_{n_s}^{(-)}\Phi^-(x_{n_s})=\varepsilon_s,s=1,\dots,2q,\) (32)

where, by (14) and (27),

\(\varepsilon_s=\lambda_{n_s}\big(F_{n_s}-x_{n_s}^{q+1}[\kappa_{n_s}^{(+)}g_q^+-\kappa_{n_s}^{(-)}g_q^-]\big)=o(N^{-q})\text{uniformly in}s.\) (33)

The leading-order behavior of \(\Delta^\pm\) is thus governed by how small the left-hand side of (32) can be, and this depends on the parity of the indices _n<sub>s</sub>_, which we study in the next subsection.

## 3.3 Parity classification and kernel basis

By (9),

\(\kappa_n^{(+)}=(-1)^nK_0+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),-\kappa_n^{(-)}=-K_0+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),\) (34)

where \(K_0=1/\sqrt{2}\). We partition the selected indices according to parity:<tbc>

\(E:=\{s\in[2q]:n_s\text{is even}\},O:=\{s\in[2q]:n_s\text{is odd}\},\)

<tbc>and set<tbc>

\(q_e:=|E|,q_o:=|O|,q_e+q_o=2q.\)

<tbc>We now examine the leading-order structure of the KEG-D coefficient matrix \(\Lambda_N\). In view of (34), define

\(\Lambda_0:=K_0\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c }
(-1)^{n_1} & (-1)^{n_1}x_{n_1} & \cdots & (-1)^{n_1}x_{n_1}^{q-1} & -1 & -x_{n_1} & \cdots & -x_{n_1}^{q-1} \\
\vdots & \vdots &  & \vdots &  & \vdots &  & \vdots \\
(-1)^{n_{2q}} & (-1)^{n_{2q}}x_{n_{2q}} & \cdots & (-1)^{n_{2q}}x_{n_{2q}}^{q-1} & -1 & -x_{n_{2q}} & \cdots & -x_{n_{2q}}^{q-1}
\end{array}\right).\)

Thus, \(\Lambda_0\) is obtained from \(\Lambda_N\) by replacing \(\kappa_{n_s}^{(+)}\) and \(-\kappa_{n_s}^{(-)}\) by their leading terms

\((-1)^{n_s}K_0\text{and}-K_0,\)

respectively. The notation \(\Lambda_0\) refers to this leading-order replacement; the matrix still depends on _N_ through the nodes _x<sub>n<sub>s</sub></sub>_.

We determine which parity distribution makes \(\Lambda_0\) non-singular. For each exponent _j_=0_,...,q_-1, consider the corresponding pair of columns

\(K_0\big((-1)^{n_s}x_{n_s}^j\big)_{s=1}^{2q},-K_0\big(x_{n_s}^j\big)_{s=1}^{2q},\)

and replace them by their sum and difference. The determinant of each such two-column transformation is -2, so the rank is unchanged.

For the sum, the _s_-th component is<tbc>

\(K_0\big((-1)^{n_s}-1\big)x_{n_s}^j=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
0, & s\in E, \\
-2K_0x_{n_s}^j, & s\in O,
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>whereas for the difference it is<tbc>

\(K_0\big((-1)^{n_s}+1\big)x_{n_s}^j=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
2K_0x_{n_s}^j, & s\in E, \\
0, & s\in O.
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>Hence, after a permutation of rows and columns, the transformed matrix has the block-diagonal form

\(\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
-2K_0V_O & 0 \\
0 & 2K_0V_E
\end{array}\right),\)

where _V<sub>O</sub>_ is the \(q_o\times q\) Vandermonde matrix on the nodes _x<sub>n<sub>s</sub></sub>_, \(s\in O\), and _V<sub>E</sub>_ is the \(q_e\times q\) Vandermonde matrix on the nodes _x<sub>n<sub>s</sub></sub>_, \(s\in E\).

For \(\Lambda_0\) to have full rank 2_q_, both _V<sub>O</sub>_ and _V<sub>E</sub>_ must have rank _q_. Hence necessarily<tbc>

\(q_o\ge q,q_e\ge q.\)

<tbc>Since<tbc>

\(q_e+q_o=2q,\)

these two inequalities hold simultaneously if and only if \(q_e=q_o=q.\) (35) Conversely, under (35), both _VE_ and _VO_ are ordinary \(q\times q\) Vandermonde matrices. Since the indices _n_1_,...,n_2_q_ are distinct, the eigenvalues \(\lambda_{n_1},\dots,\lambda_{n_{2q}}\), and hence the nodes _x__n_1_,...,x__n_2_q_, are pairwise distinct. Therefore both _VE_ and _VO_ are non-singular. Since the row and column transformations used above are invertible, it follows that \(det\Lambda_0\neq 0.\) Thus, the strict parity balance (35) is necessary and sufficient for the leading-order matrix \(\Lambda_0\) to be non-singular. This conclusion concerns \(\Lambda_0\) only; the invertibility of the actual KEG-D coefficient matrix \(\Lambda_N\) requires a separate comparison with \(\Lambda_0\). In particular, (35) explains the choice of exactly _q_ even and _q_ odd indices. We now study the leading-order structure of the error system (32). Replacing \(\kappa_{n_s}^{(+)}\) and \(\kappa_{n_s}^{(-)}\) by their leading terms from (9) and dividing by _K_0, we are led to the linear evaluation map \(\mathcal{E}:\mathcal{P}_q\times\mathcal{P}_q\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{2q},\) defined by \(\mathcal{E}(\Phi^+,\Phi^-):=\big((-1)^{n_s}\Phi^+(x_{n_s})-\Phi^-(x_{n_s})\big)_{s=1}^{2q},\) where P_q_ denotes the space of polynomials of degree at most _q_. A pair \((\Phi^+,\Phi^-)\) belongs to kerE if and only if \(W_E(x_{n_s})=0,s\in E,\)
\(W_O(x_{n_s})=0,s\in O,\) where \(W_E(x):=\Phi^+(x)-\Phi^-(x),W_O(x):=-\Phi^+(x)-\Phi^-(x).\) (36) Both _WE_ and _WO_ have degree at most _q_. We also define \(\Pi_E(x):=\prod_{s\in E}(x-x_{n_s}),\Pi_O(x):=\prod_{s\in O}(x-x_{n_s}).\) (37) **Lemma 3.1** (Kernel dimension)**.** _The kernel of_ E _has dimension_ 2 _if and only if_ \(q_e\le q+1,q_o\le q+1.\) _Proof._ The correspondence \((\Phi^+,\Phi^-)\longleftrightarrow(W_E,W_O)\) defined by (36) is a linear bijection of \(\mathcal{P}_q\times\mathcal{P}_q\) onto itself. For a pair \((\Phi^+,\Phi^-)\in ker\mathcal{E}\), the corresponding polynomial \(W_E\in\mathcal{P}_q\) must vanish at the _qe_ distinct nodes _xns_, \(s\in E\). Therefore, the space of possible _WE_ has dimension \(max\{0,q+1-q_e\}.\) Similarly, the space of possible _WO_ has dimension \(max\{0,q+1-q_o\}.\) Hence \(dimker\mathcal{E}=max\{0,q+1-q_e\}+max\{0,q+1-q_o\}.\)

<tbc>If<tbc>

\(q_e\le q+1,q_o\le q+1,\)

<tbc>then

\(\mathrm{dimker}\mathcal{E}=(q+1-q_e)+(q+1-q_o)=2,\)

because _q<sub>e</sub>+q<sub>o</sub>_=2_q_.

If, for example, \(q_e\ge q+2\), then the first term vanishes and<tbc>

\(\mathrm{dimker}\mathcal{E}=q+1-q_o.\)

<tbc>Since _q<sub>o</sub>_=2_q-q<sub>e</sub>_,

\(q+1-q_o=q_e-q+1\ge 3.\)

The case \(q_o\ge q+2\) is analogous. This proves the claim.

Under the strict-balance condition (35),<tbc>

\(|E|=|O|=q.\)

<tbc>Hence, for every \((\Phi^+,\Phi^-)\in\mathrm{ker}\mathcal{E}\),<tbc>

\(W_E=c_E\Pi_E,W_O=c_O\Pi_O,\)

<tbc>for some constants _c<sub>E</sub>,c<sub>O</sub>_. Since \(\Pi_E\) and \(\Pi_O\) are monic of degree _q_, if<tbc>

\(\Phi^\pm(x)=\sum_{k=0}^q\Phi_k^\pm x^k,\)

<tbc>then by (36),<tbc>

\(c_E=\Phi_q^+-\Phi_q^-,c_O=-\Phi_q^+-\Phi_q^-.\)

<tbc>Thus, if<tbc>

\((\Phi_q^+,\Phi_q^-)=(g^+,g^-),\)

<tbc>then<tbc>

\(W_E=(g^+-g^-)\Pi_E,W_O=(-g^+-g^-)\Pi_O.\)

<tbc>Conversely, these formulas determine \(\Phi^\pm\) uniquely through<tbc>

\(\Phi^+=\frac{W_E-W_O}{2},\Phi^-=-\frac{W_E+W_O}{2}.\)

<tbc>Therefore, the map

\((\Phi^+,\Phi^-)\longmapsto(\Phi_q^+,\Phi_q^-)\)

is a linear bijection from kerE onto C<sup>2</sup>.

We may therefore define (_U_<sup>+</sup>_,U_<sup>-</sup>) to be the unique element of kerE satisfying<tbc>

\(U_q^+=1,U_q^-=0,\)

<tbc>and (_V_ <sup>+</sup>_,V_ <sup>-</sup>) to be the unique element satisfying

\(V_q^+=0,V_q^-=1,\)

where \(U_q^\pm\) and \(V_q^\pm\) denote the coefficients of _x<sup>q</sup>_ in \(U^\pm\) and \(V^\pm\), respectively.

By (31),<tbc>

\(\Phi^\pm(x)=\Delta^\pm(x)-g_q^\pm x^q,\)

and since \(\mathrm{deg}\Delta^\pm\le q-1\), the coefficients of _x<sup>q</sup>_ in \(\Phi^\pm\) are<tbc>

\(\Phi_q^+=-g_q^+,\Phi_q^-=-g_q^-.\)

<tbc>Hence the kernel element having the same leading coefficients as the error pair \((\Phi^+,\Phi^-)\) is<tbc>

\(-g_q^+(U^+,U^-)-g_q^-(V^+,V^-).\)

<tbc>This suggests the approximation

\(\Phi^\pm(x)\approx-g_q^+U^\pm(x)-g_q^-V^\pm(x),\)

which is made precise in Lemma 3.3 and Theorem 3.4 below.

The marginal distributions<tbc>

\((q_e,q_o)=(q+1,q-1)\text{or}(q_e,q_o)=(q-1,q+1)\)

<tbc>also give

\(\mathrm{dimker}\mathcal{E}=2,\)

but they do not satisfy the leading-order non-singularity condition (35). They will therefore be considered separately in Case B below.

**Case A: strict balance** _q<sub>e</sub>=q<sub>o</sub>=q_

**Lemma 3.2.** _Under the strict-balance condition q<sub>e</sub>=q<sub>o</sub>=q,_<tbc>

\(U^+(x)=\frac{1}{2}\big[\Pi_E(x)+\Pi_O(x)\big],U^-(x)=-\frac{1}{2}\big[\Pi_E(x)-\Pi_O(x)\big],V^+(x)=-\frac{1}{2}\big[\Pi_E(x)-\Pi_O(x)\big],V^-(x)=\frac{1}{2}\big[\Pi_E(x)+\Pi_O(x)\big].\text{(38)}\)

<tbc>_Proof._ For a kernel element with coefficients of _x<sup>q</sup>_ given by (_g_<sup>+</sup>_,g_<sup>-</sup>), the preceding characterization of kerE gives<tbc>

\(W_E=(g^+-g^-)\Pi_E,W_O=(-g^+-g^-)\Pi_O.\)

<tbc>For (_U_<sup>+</sup>_,U_<sup>-</sup>), we have (_g_<sup>+</sup>_,g_<sup>-</sup>)=(1,0), and hence<tbc>

\(W_E=\Pi_E,W_O=-\Pi_O.\)

<tbc>For (_V_<sup>+</sup>_,V_<sup>-</sup>), we have (_g_<sup>+</sup>_,g_<sup>-</sup>)=(0,1), and hence<tbc>

\(W_E=-\Pi_E,W_O=-\Pi_O.\)

<tbc>Using (36), equivalently

\(\Phi^+=\frac{W_E-W_O}{2},\Phi^-=-\frac{W_E+W_O}{2},\)

gives (38).

**Case B: marginal imbalance** _qe=q_+1 **or** _qo=q_+1
Suppose first that \(q_e=q+1,q_o=q-1.\) Since \(W_E\in\mathcal{P}_q\) vanishes at _q_+1 distinct nodes, \(W_E\equiv 0\). Hence, by (36), \(\Phi^+=\Phi^-\), and therefore \(\Phi_q^+=\Phi_q^-.\) Using (31), this gives the compatibility condition \(g_q^+=g_q^-,\) which need not hold for a general _f_. Thus the leading-order system is degenerate; equivalently, \(\Lambda_0\) is singular. Any invertibility of the full KEG-D matrix must therefore come from the _O_(1_/n_)-corrections in (34). For _p=r_=0, these corrections vanish, so the coefficient matrix remains singular for every _N_. The case _qo=q_+1, _qe=q_-1 is analogous. Hence the subsequent analysis is restricted to the strict-balance condition _qe=qo=q_. Finally, for odd _q_, the symmetric choice \(\pm N,\pm(N-1),\dots\) falls into the marginal case: among the 2_q_ selected indices, _q_+1 have the same parity as _N_, while _q_-1 have the opposite parity. ## 3.4 Asymptotic estimates for \(\widetilde{g}_k^\pm-g_k^\pm\) We now restrict to the strictly balanced case and assume, in addition, that the limiting nodes are distinct within each parity class. Under these assumptions, the following lemma shows that a solution of (32) remains quantitatively close to the unique element of kerE whose coefficients of _xq_ are \(-g_q^+\) and \(-g_q^-\). **Lemma 3.3** (Stability)**.** _Assume qe=qo=q, and let the indices satisfy_ (27) _with_ \(lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n_s}{N}=c_s\neq 0,s=1,\dots,2q.\) _Assume that the numbers_ \(\{c_s:s\in E\}\) _are pairwise distinct, as are_ \(\{c_s:s\in O\}\)_. Let_ \(\Phi^\pm(x)=\sum_{k=0}^q\Phi_k^\pm x^k\) _satisfy_ (32) _with_ \(\Phi_q^\pm=-g_q^\pm,\) _and put_ \(\varepsilon:=max_s|\varepsilon_s|.\) _Then, for all sufficiently large N,_ \(\Phi_k^\pm+g_q^+U_k^\pm+g_q^-V_k^\pm=O\left(N^k\varepsilon+N^{k-q-1}\right),k=0,\dots,q-1,\) (39) _where_ \(U_k^\pm\) _and_ \(V_k^\pm\) _denote the coefficients of xk in the polynomials_ \(U^\pm\) _and_ \(V^\pm\) _given by_ (38)_. Moreover, the matrix_ \(\Lambda_N\) _is invertible for all sufficiently large N._

_Proof._ Define

\(R_E:=\Phi^+-\Phi^-+(g_q^+-g_q^-)\Pi_E,R_O:=-\Phi^+-\Phi^--(g_q^++g_q^-)\Pi_O.\) (40)

where \(\Pi_E\) and \(\Pi_O\) are given by (37). Since<tbc>

\(\Phi_q^+=-g_q^+,\Phi_q^--=-g_q^-,\)

<tbc>and \(\Pi_E,\Pi_O\) are monic polynomials of degree _q_, we have<tbc>

\(\mathrm{deg}R_E,\mathrm{deg}R_O\le q-1.\)

<tbc>Using (38), we obtain

\(\Phi^++g_q^+U^++g_q^-V^+=\frac{1}{2}(R_E-R_O),\Phi^--+g_q^+U^--+g_q^-V^--=-\frac{1}{2}(R_E+R_O).\) (41)

Thus it suffices to estimate the coefficients of _R<sub>E</sub>_ and _R<sub>O</sub>_.

By (34) and (27), we may write<tbc>

\(\kappa_{n_s}^{(+)}=(-1)^{n_s}K_0+\delta_s^+,-\kappa_{n_s}^{(-)}=-K_0+\delta_s^-,\)

<tbc>where<tbc>

\(\delta_s^\pm=O(N^{-1})\)

<tbc>uniformly in _s_. Substituting these expressions into (32), and using \(\Pi_E(x_{n_s})=0\) for \(s\in E\) and \(\Pi_O(x_{n_s})=0\) for \(s\in O\), gives

\(K_0R_E(x_{n_s})=\varepsilon_s-\delta_s^+\Phi^+(x_{n_s})-\delta_s^-\Phi^-(x_{n_s}),s\in E,K_0R_O(x_{n_s})=\varepsilon_s-\delta_s^+\Phi^+(x_{n_s})-\delta_s^-\Phi^-(x_{n_s}),s\in O.\) (42)

Set

\(m:=\mathrm{max}\left\{\mathrm{max}_{s\in E}|R_E(x_{n_s})|,\mathrm{max}_{s\in O}|R_O(x_{n_s})|\right\}.\) (43)

By (5),

\(Nx_{n_s}=\frac{N}{\lambda_{n_s}}\longrightarrow\frac{2}{\pi c_s}.\)

Hence there exist constants _C,d\>_0 such that, for all sufficiently large _N_,

\(|x_{n_s}|\le\frac{C}{N},|x_{n_s}-x_{n_t}|\ge\frac{d}{N}\) (44)

whenever \(s\neq t\) belong to the same parity class.

Let \(\ell_t^E\), \(t\in E\), be the Lagrange basis polynomials associated with the _E_-nodes. Writing<tbc>

\(\ell_t^E(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}\ell_{t,k}^Ex^k,\)

<tbc>the node estimates (44) imply

\(|\ell_t^E(y)|\le C_1,|y|\le\frac{C}{N},\ell_{t,k}^E=O(N^k),k=0,\dots,q-1.\) (45)

The same estimates hold for the Lagrange basis polynomials \(\ell_t^O\), \(t\in O\).

Since \(degR_E,degR_O\le q-1\), Lagrange interpolation gives \(R_E(x)=\sum_{t\in E}R_E(x_{n_t})\ell_t^E(x),R_O(x)=\sum_{t\in O}R_O(x_{n_t})\ell_t^O(x).\) By (43) and (45), \(|R_E(y)|+|R_O(y)|\le C_2m,|y|\le\frac{C}{N}.\) If \(R_E(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}R_{E,k}x^k,R_O(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}R_{O,k}x^k,\) then (45) also gives \(R_{E,k},R_{O,k}=O(mN^k),k=0,\dots,q-1.\) (46) For every selected node _y=xns_, the definitions of _RE_ and _RO_ give \(\Phi^+(y)=\frac{1}{2}\big[R_E(y)-R_O(y)-(g_q^+-g_q^-)\Pi_E(y)-(g_q^++g_q^-)\Pi_O(y)\big],\)
\(\Phi^-(y)=-\frac{1}{2}\big[R_E(y)+R_O(y)-(g_q^+-g_q^-)\Pi_E(y)+(g_q^++g_q^-)\Pi_O(y)\big].\) By (44) and (37), \(|\Pi_E(y)|,|\Pi_O(y)|=O(N^{-q}),\) and therefore \(|\Phi^\pm(y)|\le C_3\big(N^{-q}+m\big),y=x_{n_s}.\) (47) Combining (42) with (47) and using \(\delta_s^\pm=O(N^{-1})\), we obtain \(K_0m\le\varepsilon+C_4N^{-1}\big(N^{-q}+m\big).\) Hence, for all sufficiently large _N_, \(m\le C_5\big(\varepsilon+N^{-q-1}\big).\) (48) Combining (48) with (46), we obtain \(R_{E,k},R_{O,k}=O\big(N^k\varepsilon+N^{k-q-1}\big),k=0,\dots,q-1.\) (49) Combining (49) with (41) yields (39). It remains to prove that \(\Lambda_N\) is invertible for all sufficiently large _N_. Suppose that the homogeneous version of (30) has a solution \(\Delta^\pm\in\mathcal{P}_{q-1}.\) Then (32) holds with \(\varepsilon_s=0,g_q^\pm=0.\) Hence, by (40), \(R_E=\Delta^+-\Delta^-,R_O=-\Delta^+-\Delta^-.\) Since \(\varepsilon=0\) and \(g_q^\pm=0\), the estimate (47) reduces to \(|\Phi^\pm(y)|\le C_3m.\) Substituting this into (42) gives \(m\le\frac{C_4}{K_0N}m.\)

For sufficiently large _N_, this forces _m_=0. Thus _R<sub>E</sub>_ and _R<sub>O</sub>_ vanish at the _q_ nodes of their respective parity classes. Since<tbc>

\(degR_E,degR_O\le q-1,\)

<tbc>we have

\(R_E\equiv R_O\equiv 0.\)

Hence

\(\Delta^+=\Delta^-=0.\)

Thus the homogeneous system has only the trivial solution, and \(\Lambda_N\) is invertible for all sufficiently large _N_.

Combining Lemma 3.3 with (33), we obtain the decomposition

\(\Phi^\pm(x)=-g_q^+U^\pm(x)-g_q^-V^\pm(x)+\rho^\pm(x),\) (50)

where

\(\rho^\pm(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}\rho_k^\pm x^k,\rho_k^\pm=o(N^{k-q}),k=0,\dots,q-1.\)

In particular, the coefficient of _x<sup>q</sup>_ in \(\rho^\pm\) is exactly zero.

**Theorem 3.4.** _Suppose_<tbc>

\(f\in C^q([-1,1];\mathbb{R}^2),p,r\in C^q[-1,1],\)

<tbc>_with f_<sup>(_q_)</sup> _absolutely continuous, where_ \(q\ge 1\)_. Assume that the indices n<sub>s</sub>=n<sub>s</sub>(N_) _satisfy_ (27) _with_<tbc>

\(lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n_s}{N}=c_s\neq 0,s=1,\dots,2q,\)

<tbc>_that the strict-balance condition_ (35) _holds, and that the limits_ \(\{c_s:s\in E\}\) _are pairwise distinct, as are_ \(\{c_s:s\in O\}\)_. Then_

\(\widetilde{g}_k^\pm=g_k^\pm-g_q^+U_k^\pm-g_q^-V_k^\pm+o(N^{k-q}),k=0,\dots,q-1,\) (51)

_where_ \(U_k^\pm\) _and_ \(V_k^\pm\) _denote the coefficients of x<sup>k</sup> in the polynomials_ \(U^\pm\) _and_ \(V^\pm\) _given by_ (38)_. In particular,_<tbc>

\(\widetilde{g}_k^\pm-g_k^\pm=O(N^{k-q}),k=0,\dots,q-1.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ By Lemma 3.3, the matrix \(\Lambda_N\) is invertible for all sufficiently large _N_, so the KEG-D system has a unique solution. Moreover, by (33),<tbc>

\(\varepsilon=max_s|\varepsilon_s|=o(N^{-q}).\)

<tbc>Hence (50) gives<tbc>

\(\Phi^\pm(x)=-g_q^+U^\pm(x)-g_q^-V^\pm(x)+\rho^\pm(x),\)

<tbc>where

\(\rho^\pm(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}\rho_k^\pm x^k,\rho_k^\pm=o(N^{k-q}).\)

<tbc>By (31), for _k_=0_,...,q_-1,

\(\Phi_k^\pm=\widetilde{g}_k^\pm-g_k^\pm.\)

Comparing the coefficients of _x<sup>k</sup>_ therefore gives (51).

Finally, by (38) and the node estimates (44),

\(U_k^\pm,V_k^\pm=O(N^{k-q}),k=0,\dots,q-1.\)

The final assertion follows.

**Remark 3.5.** The distinctness assumption on the limits within each parity class excludes configurations in which several of the ratios _n<sub>s</sub>/N_ converge to the same limit within _E_ or within _O_. This is analogous to the trigonometric case considered in \[1\], where a multiplicity \(\alpha\) among the limiting values requires

\(f\in C^{q+\alpha-1}\)

with \(f^{(q+\alpha-1)}\) absolutely continuous.

One expects that (51) and the corresponding _L_<sub>2</sub>-error asymptotics remain valid for clustered configurations when the maximal multiplicity \(\alpha\) is counted separately within each parity class, provided

\(f\in C^{q+\alpha-1}([-1,1];\mathbb{R}^2),\)

with \(f^{(q+\alpha-1)}\) absolutely continuous, and _p,r_ are sufficiently smooth for the asymptotic expansions in (9) to be continued to the required order in 1_/n_.

We do not prove this extension here. As in \[1, Theorem 3.3\], further integrations by parts extending (14) would introduce the additional reduced boundary values

\(g_{q+1}^\pm,\dots,g_{q+\alpha-1}^\pm,\)

which would enter the interpolation equations through higher powers of _x<sub>n<sub>s</sub></sub>_.

## 4 Asymptotic _L_<sub>2</sub> error estimates

As in (15), define<tbc>

\(\widetilde{S}_{q,N}(f):=\widetilde{P}(x)+\sum_{|n|\le N}\widetilde{F}_nv_n(x),\)

<tbc>where<tbc>

\(\widetilde{P}(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}[G_k(x,1,0)\widetilde{f}_k(1)-G_k(x,-1,0)\widetilde{f}_k(-1)].\)

<tbc>For the reduced boundary values \(\widetilde{g}_k^\pm\) obtained from (28), we choose<tbc>

\(\widetilde{f}_k(\pm 1):=\widetilde{g}_k^\pm\left(\begin{array}{ c }
cos\gamma_\pm \\
-sin\gamma_\pm
\end{array}\right),\gamma_+=\beta,\gamma_-=\alpha,\)

<tbc>so that, consistently with (8),<tbc>

\(\left(cos\gamma_\pm-sin\gamma_\pm\right)\widetilde{f}_k(\pm 1)=\widetilde{g}_k^\pm.\)

<tbc>We then set<tbc>

\(\widetilde{P}_n:=\langle\widetilde{P},v_n\rangle_{L_2},\widetilde{F}_n:=c_n-\widetilde{P}_n.\)

<tbc>The _KEG-D error_ is defined by

\(\widetilde{R}_{q,N}(f):=f-\widetilde{S}_{q,N}(f).\)

### 4.1 Main theorem

**Theorem 4.1.** _Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.4 (in particular, the strict parity balance q<sub>e</sub>=q<sub>o</sub>=q),_

\(lim_{N\rightarrow\infty} N^{2q+1}\|\widetilde{R}_{q,N}(f)\|^2=\frac{2^{2q}}{\pi^{2q+2}}[(A+B)^2J_E+(A-B)^2J_O],\) (52)

_where A,B are the Dirac jump constants_ (17) _and_<tbc>

\(J_E:=\int_{-1}^1\prod_{s\in E}\big(x-\frac{1}{c_s}\big)^2dx,J_O:=\int_{-1}^1\prod_{s\in O}\big(x-\frac{1}{c_s}\big)^2dx.\)

_Proof._ Since \(\widetilde{F}_n\) is the generalized Fourier coefficient of \(f-\widetilde{P}\), we have \(\widetilde{R}_{q,N}(f)=\sum_{|n|>N}\widetilde{F}_nv_n.\) Hence, by Parseval, \(\|\widetilde{R}_{q,N}(f)\|^2=\sum_{|n|>N}|\widetilde{F}_n|^2.\) Since \(\widetilde{F}_n=F_n+(P_n-\widetilde{P}_n),\) we first compute the second term. By the definitions of _Pn_ and \(\widetilde{P}_n\), \(P_n-\widetilde{P}_n=-x_n[\kappa_n^{(+)}\Delta^+(x_n)-\kappa_n^{(-)}\Delta^-(x_n)]\)
\(=-x_n[\kappa_n^{(+)}\Phi^+(x_n)-\kappa_n^{(-)}\Phi^-(x_n)]\)
\(-x_n^{q+1}[\kappa_n^{(+)}g_q^+-\kappa_n^{(-)}g_q^-],\) where we used (31). Define \(\mathcal{Q}_n:=\kappa_n^{(+)}\Phi^+(x_n)-\kappa_n^{(-)}\Phi^-(x_n).\) Then (14) gives \(P_n-\widetilde{P}_n=-x_n\mathcal{Q}_n-F_n+r_n,|n|>N,\) where \(r_n=o(|n|^{-q-1})\) uniformly for |_n|\>N_. Therefore \(\widetilde{F}_n=-x_n\mathcal{Q}_n+r_n.\) (53) By (50), \(\mathcal{Q}_n=-g_q^+[\kappa_n^{(+)}U^+(x_n)-\kappa_n^{(-)}U^-(x_n)]\)
\(-g_q^-[\kappa_n^{(+)}V^+(x_n)-\kappa_n^{(-)}V^-(x_n)]\)
\(+\kappa_n^{(+)}\rho^+(x_n)-\kappa_n^{(-)}\rho^-(x_n).\) Since \(\rho^\pm(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}\rho_k^\pm x^k,\rho_k^\pm=o(N^{k-q}),\) and |_xn_|=_O(N_-1) uniformly for |_n|\>N_, it follows that \(\rho^\pm(x_n)=o(N^{-q}),\) uniformly for |_n|\>N_ as \(N\rightarrow\infty\). Using (34) and (38), we now distinguish the parity of the tail index _n_. For |_n|\>N_, we have \(U^\pm(x_n),V^\pm(x_n)=O(N^{-q}).\) Hence, if _n_ is even, \(\kappa_n^{(+)}U^+(x_n)-\kappa_n^{(-)}U^-(x_n)=K_0\Pi_E(x_n)+o(N^{-q}),\) and \(\kappa_n^{(+)}V^+(x_n)-\kappa_n^{(-)}V^-(x_n)=-K_0\Pi_E(x_n)+o(N^{-q}).\)

If _n_ is odd,<tbc>

\(\kappa_n^{(+)}U^+(x_n)-\kappa_n^{(-)}U^-(x_n)=-K_0\Pi_O(x_n)+o(N^{-q}),\)

<tbc>and<tbc>

\(\kappa_n^{(+)}V^+(x_n)-\kappa_n^{(-)}V^-(x_n)=-K_0\Pi_O(x_n)+o(N^{-q}).\)

<tbc>Hence

\(\mathcal{Q}_n=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
-K_0(g_q^++g_q^-)\Pi_E(x_n)+o(N^{-q}), & n\text{even}, \\
K_0(g_q^++g_q^-)\Pi_O(x_n)+o(N^{-q}), & n\text{odd}.
\end{array}\right.\) (54)

Combining (53) and (54), and using (37), we obtain

\(\widetilde{F}_n=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
K_0(g_q^++g_q^-)x_n^{q+1}\prod_{s\in E}\left(1-\frac{n}{n_s}\right)+x_n\sigma_{n,N}, & n\text{even}, \\
-K_0(g_q^++g_q^-)x_n^{q+1}\prod_{s\in O}\left(1-\frac{n}{n_s}\right)+x_n\sigma_{n,N}, & n\text{odd},
\end{array}\right.\) (55)

where<tbc>

\(sup_{|n|>N}|\sigma_{n,N}|=o(N^{-q}).\)

<tbc>Here we used (37) and (5). Indeed,<tbc>

\(nx_n=\frac{2}{\pi}+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),\)

<tbc>and hence, uniformly for |_n|\>N_,<tbc>

\((x_n-x_{n_s})-x_n\left(1-\frac{n}{n_s}\right)=\frac{nx_n-n_sx_{n_s}}{n_s}=O(N^{-2}).\)

<tbc>It follows that

\(x_n\Pi_E(x_n)=x_n^{q+1}\prod_{s\in E}\left(1-\frac{n}{n_s}\right)+x_nO(N^{-q-1}),\)

and analogously for \(\Pi_O\).

The remainders in (55) are of the form \(x_n\sigma_{n,N}\), where<tbc>

\(sup_{|n|>N}|\sigma_{n,N}|=o(N^{-q}).\)

<tbc>Since<tbc>

\(\sum_{|n|>N}|x_n|^2=O(N^{-1}),\)

<tbc>we have

\(\sum_{|n|>N}|x_n\sigma_{n,N}|^2=o(N^{-2q-1}).\)

The squared sum of the leading terms in (55) is _O(N_<sup>-2_q_-1</sup>), so the corresponding cross terms are also _o(N_<sup>-2_q_-1</sup>) by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Thus only the leading terms in (55) contribute to the limit.

For the even indices, the Riemann-sum argument gives

\(N^{2q+1}\sum_{|n|>Nn\text{even}}|\widetilde{F}_n|^2\longrightarrow K_0^2(g_q^+-g_q^-)^2\frac{(2/\pi)^{2q+2}}{2}\int_{|u|>1}u^{-2q-2}\prod_{s\in E}\left(1-\frac{u}{c_s}\right)^2du.\)

The factor 1/2 accounts for the density of the even integers. With the change of variables _u_=1_/x_,<tbc>

\(\int_{|u|>1}u^{-2q-2}\prod_{s\in E}\left(1-\frac{u}{c_s}\right)^2du=\int_{-1}^1\prod_{s\in E}\left(x-\frac{1}{c_s}\right)^2dx=J_E.\)

<tbc>Similarly,<tbc>

\(N^{2q+1}\sum_{|n|>N\text{odd}}|\widetilde{F}_n|^2\longrightarrow K_0^2(g_q^++g_q^-)^2\frac{(2/\pi)^{2q+2}}{2}J_O.\)

<tbc>Using \(K_0^2=1/2\), we conclude that<tbc>

\(N^{2q+1}\|\widetilde{R}_{q,N}(f)\|^2\longrightarrow\frac{2^{2q}}{\pi^{2q+2}}\left[(g_q^+-g_q^-)^2J_E+(g_q^++g_q^-)^2J_O\right].\)

<tbc>Finally, by (17),

\(g_q^+-g_q^-=A+B,g_q^++g_q^-=A-B,\)

so this is precisely (52).

**Remark 4.2.** For comparison, applying the same Riemann-sum argument to the exact-jumps coefficients _F<sub>n</sub>_ gives (18):

\(lim_{N\rightarrow\infty} N^{2q+1}\|R_{q,N}(f)\|^2=\frac{2^{2q+2}}{\pi^{2q+2}(2q+1)}(A^2+B^2).\)

Thus, so long as the parity balance holds, computing the boundary values from the generalized Fourier coefficients does not degrade the rate of convergence, but changes the asymptotic constant.
